CH12002 Tutorial Notes Benjamin J. Morgan 2026-10-30 About these notes These notes accompany the tutorial questions for Y1 Physical Chemistry at the University of Bath. They are intended to help you understand the chemistry behind the calculations—what is physically happening, and why. Throughout these notes, the emphasis is on thinking through each problem before reaching for an equation. These notes are not a replacement for the tutorial itself, nor for your lecture notes. They are a companion resource, designed to be read alongside the tutorial questions.

1 States of Matter Why is water a liquid at room temperature, when methane, a molecule of similar size, is a gas? Why does a liquid stop cooling while it freezes? Why does adding a second liquid change how much of the first one evaporates? All of these come back to two competing things: how strongly molecules attract each other, and how much kinetic energy they have to pull apart. This chapter looks at each in turn, and then puts them together. 1.1 Intermolecular interactions: which ones, and how strong? Faced with a molecule and asked about its intermolecular interactions, it is tempting to go straight to a list of forces. It helps to split the problem into two separate questions instead: Which kinds of interaction are possible? This is a yes/no question, and it is answered by the shape (and composition) of the molecule. How big is each one? This is a question of size, and it is answered by how large and polarisable the molecule is. Keeping these apart avoids a lot of confusion. The first question tells you which interactions are present; it tells you nothing about which one matters most. 1.1.1 Start with the shape Before thinking about forces at all, draw the molecule, and draw it in three dimensions. The question to ask is: does the molecule have a net (permanent) dipole? Most bonds between different atoms are polar, because one atom is more electronegative than the other. But a molecule can have polar bonds and still have no net dipole, if its symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel. \(\ce{CO2}\) is linear, so its two \(\ce{C=O}\) bond dipoles point in exactly opposite directions and cancel. \(\ce{CCl4}\) is tetrahedral, and its four \(\ce{C-Cl}\) bond dipoles cancel in the same way. Less symmetric molecules, such as bent \(\ce{H2O}\) or pyramidal \(\ce{NH3}\), keep a net dipole. This is where a flat drawing can mislead you. Draw \(\ce{CH2Br2}\) on paper with the two bromine atoms opposite each other, and it looks as though the bond dipoles should cancel. But the molecule is not flat; it is tetrahedral. Any two corners of a tetrahedron are equivalent, so there is only one \(\ce{CH2Br2}\), and it always has a net dipole. A quick 3D sketch (or a model kit) settles questions like this straight away. Polar bonds do not guarantee a polar molecule. Whether the bond dipoles cancel depends on the three-dimensional shape, so draw the shape first and deduce the properties from it. “No net dipole” does not mean the charge is spread perfectly evenly, though. In \(\ce{CO2}\) the oxygen ends are still slightly negative and the middle slightly positive; the arrangement simply has no overall direction. A neighbouring molecule that comes very close can feel some of that unevenness. It is a much smaller effect than a genuine dipole, but it is one reason symmetric molecules built from polar bonds can be a little “stickier” than their size alone would suggest. 1.1.2 Which interactions are possible? Once you know whether the molecule has a net dipole, the possible interactions follow: Interaction What it needs Dispersion Nothing: present between all atoms and molecules Dipole–dipole Both molecules have a net dipole Dipole–induced dipole At least one molecule has a net dipole Hydrogen bonding An H bonded to N, O or F on one molecule, and a lone pair on N, O or F on another Dispersion is always there. The electron cloud of any molecule fluctuates, and at any instant it has a small, temporary dipole. That temporary dipole distorts the electron cloud of a neighbour, and the two fluctuations become correlated in a way that leads to attraction. Even helium atoms attract each other like this, which is why helium can be liquefied at all. Dipole–induced dipole interactions are easy to forget. A molecule with a permanent dipole produces an electric field, and that field distorts the electron cloud of any neighbour, polar or not, inducing an extra dipole in it. This happens between two polar molecules too: each molecule’s permanent dipole induces an additional dipole in the other, on top of the permanent one. So two polar molecules attract each other in three ways, not two. Hydrogen bonding needs both a donor (an H attached to N, O or F) and an acceptor (a lone pair on N, O or F). Acetone, \(\ce{(CH3)2CO}\), has an acceptor (the carbonyl oxygen) but no donor, so acetone molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other, even though acetone is strongly polar. Dispersion is always present. If a molecule has a net dipole, it has dipole–dipole and dipole–induced dipole interactions. Hydrogen bonding needs a donor and an acceptor. 1.1.3 Then ask: how big? Knowing which interactions are present does not yet tell you which one matters most. For that, you need to think about size. Dispersion grows with polarisability: how easily the electron cloud can be distorted. Bigger molecules have bigger electron clouds, with outer electrons held further from the nuclei, and these are more easily pushed around. The number of electrons is a useful rough guide, since more electrons usually means a bigger, more polarisable molecule. It is only a guide, though: what really matters is how loosely the outer electrons are held. The noble gases show this cleanly, because dispersion is the only interaction they have. Their boiling points rise steadily with size: He (−269 °C), Ne (−246 °C), Ar (−186 °C), Kr (−153 °C), Xe (−108 °C). Shape matters too. Pentane (boiling point 36 °C) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (9.5 °C) have the same formula, \(\ce{C5H12}\), and the same number of electrons. But pentane is a long chain that can lie alongside its neighbours, with lots of close contact, while 2,2-dimethylpropane is a compact ball that can only touch its neighbours at a few points. More contact means more dispersion. So which contribution is usually the biggest? For most molecules, including most polar ones, it is dispersion. Look at the hydrogen halides: Dipole moment / D Boiling point / °C \(\ce{HCl}\) 1.08 −85 \(\ce{HBr}\) 0.82 −67 \(\ce{HI}\) 0.44 −35 If dipole–dipole interactions were the main attraction, \(\ce{HCl}\) would boil highest. It boils lowest. Going down the group the molecules get bigger and more polarisable, and dispersion grows faster than the dipole shrinks. Two more comparisons make the same point. \(\ce{CO}\) and \(\ce{N2}\) have the same number of electrons and very similar polarisabilities, but \(\ce{CO}\) is polar and \(\ce{N2}\) is not. Their boiling points are −191.5 °C and −195.8 °C: the dipole is there, but it adds almost nothing. And non-polar \(\ce{CCl4}\) (77 °C) boils about 100 °C higher than polar \(\ce{CH3Cl}\) (−24 °C), because it is a much bigger molecule. You may have met dispersion forces at A-level as London forces; they are the same thing. You may also have met a ranking along the lines of “London forces < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding”. That ranking captures something real: compare two molecules of similar size, and the one with a dipole, or with hydrogen bonding, will usually boil higher. But it is easy to read it as saying that dispersion is always the smallest contribution, and that is not true. For most molecules, dispersion is the largest contribution to the attraction, even when the molecule is polar. Dipoles and hydrogen bonds make a visible difference mainly when you compare molecules of similar size. 1.1.4 When do dipoles decide? So when do dipoles and hydrogen bonds show up? Most clearly when dispersion is held roughly constant: when you compare molecules of similar size and shape. Consider three molecules with almost the same molar mass: \(M\) / g mol−1 \(\alpha\) / \(10^{-24}\) cm3 \(\mu\) / D Boiling point / °C Butane, \(\ce{CH3CH2CH2CH3}\) 58 8.2 0 −1 Acetone, \(\ce{(CH3)2CO}\) 58 6.4 2.9 56 Propan-1-ol, \(\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}\) 60 6.7 1.6 97 Before explaining the trend, check what each column is doing. The polarisability, if anything, goes down from butane to the other two, so dispersion cannot be what pushes the boiling point up. Acetone’s large dipole lifts it well above butane. Propan-1-ol has a smaller dipole than acetone, yet boils higher still, because its \(\ce{O-H}\) group lets it hydrogen bond, which acetone cannot do. This is a useful habit whenever you are given a table of molecular properties: look at how each property varies before reaching for an explanation. If the polarisability barely changes, dispersion is not the story, and the differences must come from something else. 1.1.5 A note on SO3: when the categories blur The two-question approach works well for most molecules, but the categories are not always clean. Sulfur trioxide is a good example. \(\ce{SO3}\) is trigonal planar, so it has no net dipole, yet it boils at 45 °C, well above polar \(\ce{SO2}\) (−10 °C). Part of the reason is size: \(\ce{SO3}\) has more electrons, and so stronger dispersion. But there is more going on. The sulfur in \(\ce{SO3}\) is very electron-poor: it is bonded to three electronegative oxygens and has no lone pair of its own. Because the molecule is flat, that sulfur is exposed above and below the plane. A lone pair on an oxygen of a neighbouring molecule can approach face-on and bond to it, forming an \(\ce{S-O-S}\) bridge. Three molecules can link up like this into a ring, \(\ce{S3O9}\), and liquid \(\ce{SO3}\) is a mixture of single molecules and these rings. So boiling \(\ce{SO3}\) involves more than overcoming dispersion between separate molecules: some of what holds the liquid together is closer to weak covalent bonding. The categories of intermolecular interaction are a very useful way to organise your thinking, but molecules do not always stay as the separate units we draw. When a substance behaves unexpectedly, it is worth asking whether the liquid is really made of the molecule you drew. 1.2 Kinetic theory: what temperature and pressure mean 1.2.1 Temperature and kinetic energy In a gas, molecules fly around freely, colliding with each other and with the walls. Kinetic theory tells us that the average translational kinetic energy per molecule is \[\langle E_\mathrm{k} \rangle = \tfrac{3}{2} k_\mathrm{B} T\] Notice what is not in this equation: anything about the molecule. A light \(\ce{H2}\) molecule and a heavy \(\ce{CO2}\) molecule at the same temperature have the same average kinetic energy. Why should that be? Think about what happens in a mixture of gases. Molecules collide constantly, and each collision passes energy from one molecule to another. A fast, light molecule and a slow, heavy one keep exchanging energy until, on average, neither kind is gaining at the other’s expense. At that point their average kinetic energies are equal. That shared average is exactly what temperature measures: two things are at the same temperature when, in contact, there is no net flow of energy between them. For a gas, \(\tfrac{3}{2}k_\mathrm{B}T\) tells you how big that average is. Since \(\langle E_\mathrm{k} \rangle = \tfrac{1}{2}m\langle v^2 \rangle\), equal kinetic energies mean that heavier molecules must move more slowly. The root mean square speed is \[v_\mathrm{rms} = \sqrt{\langle v^2 \rangle} = \sqrt{\frac{3k_\mathrm{B}T}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}\] This depends only on temperature and molar mass. It does not depend on pressure: squeezing a gas at constant temperature makes its molecules collide more often, but it does not make them move any faster. In \(v_\mathrm{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}\), the molar mass must be in kg mol−1, because a joule is a kg m2 s−2. A quick sense check helps: \(\ce{N2}\) at 25 °C has \(v_\mathrm{rms} \approx 515~\text{m s}^{-1}\), similar to the speed of sound in air. If you get a few metres per second, or tens of thousands, check your units. 1.2.2 What is pressure? Pressure is the push of molecules hitting the walls of their container. Each collision transfers momentum to the wall, and the pressure is the momentum delivered per unit area per unit time. Think about how this depends on the molecules. A molecule moving at speed \(v\) carries momentum proportional to \(mv\), so it hits harder the faster and heavier it is. It also hits the walls more often the faster it moves, at a rate proportional to \(v\). Put these together and the pressure goes as \(mv^2\), which is kinetic energy. Working through the geometry carefully (and averaging over all three directions) gives \[p = \frac{1}{3}\frac{N}{V} m\langle v^2 \rangle = \frac{2}{3}\times\frac{\text{total translational kinetic energy}}{V}\] So pressure is kinetic energy per unit volume, up to a factor of \(\tfrac{2}{3}\). The units already say so: \(1~\text{Pa} = 1~\text{N m}^{-2} = 1~\text{J m}^{-3}\). Rearranging gives a neat result: the total translational kinetic energy of a gas is \(\tfrac{3}{2}pV\). For example, the air in a 1 L flask at 1 atm has \[E_\mathrm{k,total} = \tfrac{3}{2} \times 101325~\text{Pa} \times 1.0\times10^{-3}~\text{m}^3 \approx 150~\text{J}\] of translational kinetic energy, and you can work this out without counting a single molecule. This picture also explains Dalton’s law of partial pressures. A heavy, slow molecule hits the wall less often but harder; a light, fast molecule hits more often but more gently. Because both carry the same average kinetic energy, these effects balance exactly, and every molecule contributes equally to the pressure, whatever its mass. So each gas in a mixture contributes to the pressure in proportion to how many molecules of it there are: its partial pressure is its mole fraction times the total pressure. Pressure is two-thirds of the translational kinetic energy per unit volume. At a fixed temperature every molecule pushes on the walls equally hard on average, so pressure effectively counts molecules per unit volume. 1.2.3 Why can we usually ignore interactions in a gas? The same intermolecular interactions are present in a gas as in a liquid. So why does the ideal gas law, which ignores them, work so well? At 1 atm and room temperature, gas molecules are on average about 3 nm apart, roughly ten times their own size. Dispersion interactions fall off very steeply with distance, as \(r^{-6}\), so ten times further away means about a million times weaker. The interactions are still there; they are just too weak at these distances to matter much. They become important when a gas is compressed or cooled, bringing the molecules closer together, which is exactly when gases condense. 1.3 Phase changes and cooling curves 1.3.1 Why does the temperature stop falling? If you let a pure liquid cool and record its temperature over time, the temperature falls steadily at first. Then, at the freezing point, it stops falling and stays constant for a while, even though the substance is still losing energy to its surroundings. Only once all the liquid has solidified does the temperature start to fall again. On that plateau the temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy of the molecules is constant too. So where is the energy that flows out to the surroundings coming from? From the intermolecular interactions. As molecules lock into place in the solid, they settle into lower-energy positions alongside their neighbours, and the energy released is the latent heat of fusion. That released energy is what flows out to the surroundings while the temperature holds steady. It is worth being careful about the direction here. Freezing releases energy, because interactions are forming. Melting absorbs exactly the same amount, because those interactions have to be broken. On a plateau, energy is still flowing, but it is changing the energy of the intermolecular interactions rather than the kinetic energy of the molecules. Freezing releases latent heat; melting absorbs it. 1.3.2 Supercooling Sometimes a liquid cools below its freezing point without solidifying. Crystals need somewhere to start growing: a nucleation site, such as a speck of dust, a scratch on the container, or a seed crystal. A very pure liquid in a very clean container may have none, so it stays liquid below its freezing point. Once a crystal does start, it grows quickly, releasing latent heat, and the temperature rises back up to the freezing point. On a cooling curve, supercooling shows up as a small dip below the plateau temperature just before the plateau begins. 1.4 Mixtures and Raoult’s law 1.4.1 What does vapour pressure measure? Every liquid is in equilibrium with its vapour: molecules escape from the surface, and molecules in the vapour return. The vapour pressure is the pressure of the vapour once this equilibrium is reached. What does that number tell you physically? Rearrange the ideal gas law, \(pV = nRT\), to give \[p = \frac{n}{V}\,RT\] At a fixed temperature, then, the vapour pressure is proportional to \(n/V\): the number of moles (and so the number of molecules) per unit volume in the vapour. It measures how concentrated the vapour is. Notice that this is a concentration, not an amount. A bigger container holds more vapour, but not at a higher pressure: more molecules evaporate to fill the extra space, until the concentration is back where it was. Vapour pressure is an intensive property. It depends on the liquid and the temperature, not on how much liquid there is or how big the container is (as long as some liquid remains). 1.4.2 What does “saturated” mean? Questions sometimes refer to the saturated vapour pressure. This is the same quantity we have been calling the vapour pressure: the pressure of the vapour when it is in equilibrium with the liquid. The word “saturated” makes that condition explicit. At this pressure the vapour holds as much of the substance as it can at that temperature, and adding any more would just make some of it condense. Why would a question bother to say so? Because the vapour of a substance is not always in equilibrium with its liquid. The partial pressure of a substance actually present in a gas can be: Below the saturated vapour pressure (unsaturated). If there is liquid present, more evaporates until the pressure rises to the saturated value. Relative humidity is exactly this ratio for water: air at 50% relative humidity contains water vapour at half its saturated vapour pressure, which is why wet clothes dry. Above the saturated vapour pressure (supersaturated). This is not an equilibrium state, but it can persist if there is nowhere for droplets to start forming, much like a supercooled liquid. Clouds form when supersaturated water vapour condenses onto tiny particles of dust or salt, which act as nucleation sites. This also explains the “as long as some liquid remains” caveat above. Once all the liquid has evaporated, there is nothing left to top up the vapour. Expand the container further and the vapour becomes unsaturated, with its pressure falling below the saturated value. In Raoult’s law, every pressure is an equilibrium value: \(p^\circ_\mathrm{A}\) is the saturated vapour pressure of pure A, and \(p_\mathrm{A}\) is the equilibrium partial pressure of A above the mixture. Qualifiers such as “saturated”, “standard” or “isothermal” tell you about a condition that holds in the problem. When a question includes one, it is worth pausing to ask what it rules in or out. “Saturated” means the vapour is in equilibrium with the liquid. 1.4.3 Raoult’s law as a balance Now mix two liquids, A and B, and think about the A molecules. At equilibrium, A molecules leave the liquid at the same rate as they return. Leaving: only molecules at the surface can escape. If an A molecule’s chance of escaping is the same as it would be in pure A, the rate of escape is simply proportional to how much of the liquid is A, its mole fraction \(x_\mathrm{A}\). Returning: the rate at which A molecules hit the surface and rejoin the liquid is proportional to how many there are in the vapour, which goes as \(p_\mathrm{A}\). Balancing the two gives \(p_\mathrm{A} \propto x_\mathrm{A}\). For pure A (\(x_\mathrm{A} = 1\)) the vapour pressure must be \(p^\circ_\mathrm{A}\), which fixes the constant: \[p_\mathrm{A} = x_\mathrm{A}\,p^\circ_\mathrm{A}\] This is Raoult’s law. The total vapour pressure is the sum of the two contributions, \(p = x_\mathrm{A}\,p^\circ_\mathrm{A} + x_\mathrm{B}\,p^\circ_\mathrm{B}\), which is a straight line between \(p^\circ_\mathrm{B}\) and \(p^\circ_\mathrm{A}\) on a plot of pressure against composition. The key assumption was that an A molecule’s chance of escaping does not depend on whether its neighbours are A or B. That is what makes a mixture ideal: the A–B interactions are the same as the A–A and B–B ones, so the molecules effectively cannot tell each other apart. Mixtures of very similar molecules, such as benzene and toluene, come close to this. Raoult’s law says that each component’s vapour is diluted in proportion to its share of the liquid. It holds when the molecules cannot tell each other apart. 1.4.4 Deviations from ideality In a real mixture, we write \[p_\mathrm{A} = \gamma_\mathrm{A}\,x_\mathrm{A}\,p^\circ_\mathrm{A}\] where \(\gamma_\mathrm{A}\) is the activity coefficient of A. What does it mean physically? \(\gamma_\mathrm{A} < 1\) (negative deviation): the vapour pressure is lower than ideal, so A molecules are being held in the liquid more strongly than in pure A. The A–B attractions are stronger than the A–A and B–B ones. Acetone and chloroform are a good example. Neither pure liquid has significant hydrogen bonding, but in the mixture the \(\ce{C-H}\) of chloroform can hydrogen bond to the oxygen of acetone, so mixing creates new attractions. \(\gamma_\mathrm{A} > 1\) (positive deviation): the vapour pressure is higher than ideal, because the A–B attractions are weaker. Mixing ethanol with hexane is an example: hexane molecules get in between the ethanol molecules and break up ethanol’s hydrogen-bonded network, so ethanol escapes more easily. Each component of a mixture has its own activity coefficient. If you only know the total vapour pressure, the ratio \(p_\text{real}/p_\text{ideal}\) tells you the overall direction and size of the deviation (an average over both components), but not the activity coefficient of either one separately. 1.5 Summary Split questions about intermolecular interactions in two. Which interactions are possible depends on the 3D shape and composition. How big each one is depends on size and polarisability. Polar bonds do not guarantee a polar molecule: symmetry can make the bond dipoles cancel. Draw the shape in 3D first. Dispersion is always present and is usually the largest contribution, even for polar molecules. A net dipole brings dipole–dipole and dipole–induced dipole interactions; hydrogen bonding needs a donor and an acceptor. Dipoles and hydrogen bonds decide the order mainly when molecules are of similar size. \(\langle E_\mathrm{k} \rangle = \tfrac{3}{2}k_\mathrm{B}T\) for every molecule, whatever its mass, so heavier molecules move more slowly. \(v_\mathrm{rms}\) depends on \(T\) and \(M\), not on pressure. Pressure is kinetic energy per unit volume (times \(\tfrac{2}{3}\)): the total translational kinetic energy of a gas is \(\tfrac{3}{2}pV\). On a cooling curve plateau, the kinetic energy is constant while latent heat is released as intermolecular interactions form. Vapour pressure measures the concentration of molecules in the vapour. Raoult’s law follows from balancing escape and return; deviations (\(\gamma \neq 1\)) tell you whether the mixed interactions are stronger or weaker than in the pure liquids.

3 Ions and Solutions 3.1 pH and neutrality You have probably been taught that “neutral water has pH 7”. This is true at 25 °C, but it is not a general rule. To understand why, we need to think about what is actually happening in liquid water. 3.1.1 The autoionisation of water Water molecules constantly react with each other: \[\ce{2H2O <=> H3O+ + OH-}\] This is an equilibrium, and like all equilibria it is described by an equilibrium constant: \[K_\mathrm{w} = [\ce{H+}][\ce{OH-}]\] At 25 °C, \(K_\mathrm{w} = 10^{-14}\). This equilibrium lies very far to the left: only a tiny fraction of water molecules are ionised at any instant. But it is always there, and it is the reason that pure water contains any \(\ce{H+}\) or \(\ce{OH-}\) at all. 3.1.2 Why does \(K_\mathrm{w}\) change with temperature? The autoionisation is endothermic (\(\Delta H > 0\)): it costs energy to break an \(\ce{O-H}\) bond and separate charge. By Le Chatelier’s principle, raising the temperature shifts an endothermic equilibrium to the right. So at higher temperatures, more water molecules dissociate, and \(K_\mathrm{w}\) gets larger. At 100 °C, \(\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{w} \approx 12\), meaning \(K_\mathrm{w} \approx 10^{-12}\). This is 100 times larger than at 25 °C, so there really is more \(\ce{H+}\) and more \(\ce{OH-}\) in hot water. 3.1.3 What does “neutral” actually mean? Think about what we mean physically. In pure water, every \(\ce{H+}\) ion is produced alongside an \(\ce{OH-}\) ion (they come from the same autoionisation reaction). There is no other source of either ion. So in pure water, \([\ce{H+}] = [\ce{OH-}]\), always, at any temperature. A neutral solution is one where \([\ce{H+}] = [\ce{OH-}]\). That is the definition of neutrality. It is not defined as pH \(= 7\). Since \([\ce{H+}] = [\ce{OH-}]\) and \([\ce{H+}][\ce{OH-}] = K_\mathrm{w}\), we can write: \[[\ce{H+}]^2 = K_\mathrm{w}, \qquad [\ce{H+}] = \sqrt{K_\mathrm{w}}, \qquad \text{pH} = \frac{\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{w}}{2}\] At 25 °C: \(\text{pH} = 14/2 = 7\). At 100 °C: \(\text{pH} = 12/2 = 6\). Boiling water has pH 6, but it is perfectly neutral. There is equal \(\ce{H+}\) and \(\ce{OH-}\). There is just more of both, because the endothermic autoionisation is favoured at higher temperature. Note on the calculation: If we are told only \(K_\mathrm{w}\), we need to assume neutrality (\([\ce{H+}] = [\ce{OH-}]\)) in order to calculate a pH. Without this assumption, we only know the product \([\ce{H+}][\ce{OH-}]\), not the individual concentrations. For pure water this assumption is justified; for a solution containing an acid or base, it would not be. 3.2 Buffer solutions 3.2.1 What is in a buffer solution? Consider a buffer made from 0.1 mol of acetic acid (\(\ce{CH3COOH}\), a weak acid, which we abbreviate \(\ce{HA}\)) and 0.1 mol of sodium acetate (\(\ce{CH3COONa}\)), dissolved in 1 L of water. Before thinking about any equations, let us think about what is physically present in the solution: The acetic acid (\(\ce{HA}\)) is a weak acid. It does not fully dissociate. The equilibrium \(\ce{HA <=> H+ + A-}\) lies well to the left (\(K_\mathrm{a} \sim 10^{-5}\)). So most of the acetic acid sits in solution as intact \(\ce{HA}\) molecules. The sodium acetate is a salt. It dissociates completely: \(\ce{CH3COONa -> Na+ + CH3COO-}\). The \(\ce{Na+}\) is a spectator ion; it plays no further role. The \(\ce{CH3COO-}\) (which we call \(\ce{A-}\)) is the conjugate base of acetic acid. So we have deliberately placed both \(\ce{HA}\) and \(\ce{A-}\) into the solution, each at a known concentration. This is the essential feature of a buffer: a reservoir of weak acid and its conjugate base, both present in significant amounts. Why doesn’t the \(\ce{A-}\) just react with water to form \(\ce{HA}\)? It does, partially. The system reaches equilibrium, but \(K_\mathrm{a} \sim 10^{-5}\) means the equilibrium concentration of \(\ce{H+}\) is tiny (\(\sim 10^{-5}\) M). The amount of \(\ce{A-}\) that converts to \(\ce{HA}\) is negligible compared to the 0.1 mol we put in. When the buffer concentrations (\(\sim 0.1\) M) are huge compared to \(K_\mathrm{a}\) (\(\sim 10^{-5}\)), the stoichiometric amounts we put in are an excellent approximation to the equilibrium amounts. 3.2.2 Why does a buffer resist pH changes? The key idea is that the buffer has chemical reservoirs that can neutralise added acid or base. Adding acid: Suppose you add a small amount of strong acid (say \(\ce{HCl}\)). The \(\ce{HCl}\) dissociates completely, releasing \(\ce{H+}\) ions. But these \(\ce{H+}\) ions do not simply accumulate in solution. The conjugate base \(\ce{A-}\) reacts with them: \[\ce{H+ + A- -> HA}\] The \(\ce{A-}\) “mops up” the added \(\ce{H+}\), converting it into undissociated \(\ce{HA}\). Why does this happen? Because \(K_\mathrm{a}\) is small (\(\sim 10^{-5}\)), the equilibrium \(\ce{HA <=> H+ + A-}\) strongly favours the left-hand side. Adding \(\ce{H+}\) pushes the equilibrium even further to the left (Le Chatelier), so the reaction goes essentially to completion. The result: the amount of free \(\ce{H+}\) barely changes. Instead, you have slightly less \(\ce{A-}\) and slightly more \(\ce{HA}\). Adding base: If you add \(\ce{OH-}\) instead, the weak acid neutralises it: \[\ce{OH- + HA -> A- + H2O}\] Now you have slightly less \(\ce{HA}\) and slightly more \(\ce{A-}\), but the pH barely changes. A buffer works because the conjugate base mops up added \(\ce{H+}\), and the weak acid neutralises added \(\ce{OH-}\). The buffer is overwhelmed only when you run out of one of these reservoirs. 3.2.3 The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation This is not a new equation to memorise. It is simply the \(K_\mathrm{a}\) expression, rearranged: \[K_\mathrm{a} = \frac{[\ce{H+}][\ce{A-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}\] \[[\ce{H+}] = K_\mathrm{a}\,\frac{[\ce{HA}]}{[\ce{A-}]}\] \[\text{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a} + \log\!\left(\frac{[\ce{A-}]}{[\ce{HA}]}\right)\] When \([\ce{A-}] = [\ce{HA}]\), the log term vanishes and \(\text{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}\). This is the optimal buffer: you have equal amounts of acid and base available, so you are equally well prepared for added acid or added base. 3.2.4 Thinking through a buffer problem Rather than blindly plugging into the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, it is better to think step by step about what happens physically. Consider adding 0.01 mol of \(\ce{HCl}\) to 1 L of the acetic acid buffer described above: \(\ce{HCl}\) dissociates completely (it is a strong acid): \(\ce{HCl -> H+ + Cl-}\). We now have 0.01 mol of extra \(\ce{H+}\). The conjugate base mops up the \(\ce{H+}\): The \(\ce{A-}\) reacts with the added \(\ce{H+}\) to form \(\ce{HA}\), and this goes essentially to completion (because \(K_\mathrm{a}\) is small). So 0.01 mol of \(\ce{A-}\) is consumed, and 0.01 mol of \(\ce{HA}\) is produced. Work out the new concentrations: \[\begin{align*} [\ce{A-}] &= 0.10 - 0.01 = 0.09~\text{M} \\ [\ce{HA}] &= 0.10 + 0.01 = 0.11~\text{M} \end{align*}\] Now use Henderson–Hasselbalch: \[\text{pH} = 4.756 + \log\!\left(\frac{0.09}{0.11}\right) = 4.756 - 0.087 = 4.669\] The pH has shifted by less than 0.1 units, despite adding a significant amount of strong acid. Compare: adding 0.01 mol of \(\ce{HCl}\) to 1 L of pure water would give \(\text{pH} \approx 2\). 3.2.5 The stoichiometric approximation In Step 3 above, we used the stoichiometric concentrations (0.09 and 0.11 M) as though they were the true equilibrium concentrations. Strictly, a tiny amount of the \(\ce{HA}\) will dissociate back to \(\ce{H+}\) and \(\ce{A-}\) at equilibrium. To get the exact answer you would need to solve a quadratic. But because \(K_\mathrm{a}\) (\(\sim 10^{-5}\)) is so much smaller than the buffer concentrations (\(\sim 0.1\) M), the equilibrium shift is negligible. This is why buffer problems typically say “estimate the pH”: we are making a deliberate, physically justified approximation. 3.3 Activity and ionic strength 3.3.1 The problem with concentrations Up to this point we have been using concentrations directly in our equilibrium expressions: \(K_\mathrm{a} = [\ce{H+}][\ce{A-}]/[\ce{HA}]\), \(K_\mathrm{w} = [\ce{H+}][\ce{OH-}]\), and so on. This works well for dilute solutions of uncharged molecules. But for ions, there is a problem. 3.3.2 The ionic atmosphere: a physical picture In an ionic solution, every ion is surrounded by other ions. Electrostatics dictates that oppositely charged ions tend to cluster nearby: a positive ion will, on average, have slightly more negative ions in its vicinity than positive ones. This surrounding cloud of (predominantly) opposite charge is called the ionic atmosphere. The ionic atmosphere partially stabilises the central ion. Think of it this way: the ion sits in a favourable electrostatic environment, a potential energy well created by the surrounding charges. To participate in a chemical reaction, the ion would need to leave this stabilising environment. There is an energetic cost to doing so. The practical consequence is that a stabilised ion is less reactive than a free ion would be. An \(\ce{H+}\) ion surrounded by its ionic atmosphere is less available to react with a base, donate to a proton transfer, or do anything else chemical. It behaves as though its concentration were lower than it actually is. The ionic atmosphere stabilises ions in solution. A more stabilised ion has a greater energetic cost to participate in chemistry, so it behaves as though its concentration is lower than it really is. 3.3.3 Activity: quantifying the effect We formalise this using the concept of activity. The activity of an ion is its “effective concentration”: the concentration it appears to have, based on its chemical behaviour: \[a = \gamma \, c\] where \(c\) is the actual (stoichiometric) concentration and \(\gamma\) is the activity coefficient. In an ideal (very dilute) solution: \(\gamma = 1\), so \(a = c\) and concentrations work fine. In a real solution with significant ion–ion interactions: \(\gamma < 1\), so \(a < c\). The ion is “less active” than its concentration suggests. For pH, this means we should really write: \[\text{pH} = -\log(a_{\ce{H+}}) = -\log(\gamma\,[\ce{H+}])\] A lower \(\gamma\) gives a higher pH (less acidic) than the concentration alone would predict. 3.3.4 Ionic strength: what controls the ionic atmosphere? The strength of the ionic atmosphere depends on two things: how many ions are nearby, and how charged they are. A doubly-charged ion creates a much stronger electrostatic field than a singly-charged one, and therefore contributes more to the ionic atmosphere of every other ion in the solution. This is quantified by the ionic strength, \(I\): \[I = \frac{1}{2}\sum_i c_i\,z_i^2\] where the sum runs over all ions, \(c_i\) is the concentration of ion \(i\), and \(z_i\) is its charge. Notice the \(z_i^2\) weighting: a \(\ce{SO4^{2-}}\) ion contributes four times as much to the ionic strength as a \(\ce{Cl-}\) ion at the same concentration, because \((2)^2 = 4\) versus \((1)^2 = 1\). This reflects the physical reality that a more highly charged ion has a stronger electrostatic effect on its surroundings. 3.3.5 The Debye–Hückel limiting law The Debye–Hückel limiting law gives us a quantitative estimate of how much the ionic atmosphere reduces \(\gamma\): \[\log\gamma_{\pm} = -0.509\,|z_+\,z_-|\,\sqrt{I}\] This equation encodes the physics we have been discussing: Higher ionic strength \(\to\) smaller \(\gamma\): More ions means a denser ionic atmosphere, which stabilises each ion more, making it less chemically active. Higher charges \(\to\) smaller \(\gamma\): More highly charged ions interact more strongly, so the stabilisation effect is larger. \(\sqrt{I}\) dependence: This comes from the physics of electrostatic screening (the Debye screening length scales as \(1/\sqrt{I}\)). The equation is valid for dilute solutions (\(I \lesssim 0.01\) M). At higher concentrations, the simple model breaks down and more sophisticated theories are needed. 3.3.6 Example: why do HCl and H2SO4 differ? Consider 0.01 M \(\ce{HCl}\) and 0.005 M \(\ce{H2SO4}\). Ideally, both produce \([\ce{H+}] = 0.01\) M and pH \(= 2\). But in reality, the \(\ce{H2SO4}\) solution has a slightly higher pH (is less acidic). Why? Stronger ionic atmosphere: \(\ce{H2SO4}\) contains the doubly-charged \(\ce{SO4^{2-}}\) ion, which contributes more to the ionic strength (\(I = 0.015\) M) than the singly-charged \(\ce{Cl-}\) in \(\ce{HCl}\) (\(I = 0.01\) M). A higher ionic strength means a stronger ionic atmosphere, a smaller \(\gamma\), and therefore a higher pH. Incomplete dissociation: \(\ce{H2SO4}\) is dibasic. The first proton comes off completely, but the second does not. The solution contains a mixture of \(\ce{HSO4-}\) and \(\ce{SO4^{2-}}\). So there are fewer free \(\ce{H+}\) ions than the ideal calculation predicts. 3.3.7 Worked example: applying the Debye–Hückel limiting law Let us put numbers to the ionic atmosphere effect for 0.01 M \(\ce{HCl}\). Identify the ions and their charges. \(\ce{HCl}\) dissociates completely: \([\ce{H+}] = [\ce{Cl-}] = 0.01\) M, with charges \(z_+ = +1\) and \(z_- = -1\). Calculate the ionic strength. \[I = \tfrac{1}{2}(0.01 \times 1^2 + 0.01 \times 1^2) = 0.01~\text{M}\] Apply the Debye–Hückel limiting law. \[\log\gamma = -0.509 \times |{+1} \times {-1}| \times \sqrt{0.01} = -0.509 \times 1 \times 0.1 = -0.0509\] Find \(\gamma\). \[\gamma = 10^{-0.0509} = 0.889\] The activity of \(\ce{H+}\) is about 89% of its concentration. The ionic atmosphere reduces its effective concentration by about 11%. Calculate the pH. \[\text{pH} = -\log(\gamma \times [\ce{H+}]) = -\log(0.889 \times 0.01) = -\log(0.00889) = 2.051\] This is slightly higher than the ideal pH of 2.000, as we expected: the ionic atmosphere stabilises the \(\ce{H+}\), making it less active. Shortcut: Since \(\text{pH} = -\log\gamma - \log[\ce{H+}] = -\log\gamma + 2\), the correction to pH is simply \(-\log\gamma = 0.051\). So \(\text{pH} = 2 + 0.051 = 2.051\). 3.4 Osmotic pressure and PBS 3.4.1 What is osmotic pressure? When a solution is separated from pure solvent by a semi-permeable membrane (one that lets solvent through but not solute), solvent flows into the solution by osmosis. The osmotic pressure \(\Pi\) is the pressure you would need to apply to the solution to stop this flow. Osmotic pressure is a colligative property: it depends only on the total number of dissolved particles, not on their identity, charge, or mass. Every dissolved ion or molecule contributes equally. The osmotic pressure is: \[\Pi = cRT\] where \(c\) is the total concentration of all dissolved species. Use the total particle concentration for osmotic pressure, not the ionic strength. Ionic strength weights by charge squared; it measures the electrostatic environment. Osmotic pressure just counts particles. This is a common source of error. A note on the van ’t Hoff factor. Some textbooks write the osmotic pressure as \(\Pi = iMRT\), where \(M\) is the formula concentration of the salt (e.g. 0.135 M for \(\ce{NaCl}\)) and \(i\) is the van ’t Hoff factor, the number of ions produced per formula unit (\(i = 2\) for \(\ce{NaCl}\), \(i = 3\) for \(\ce{Na2HPO4}\), etc.). This is equivalent to what we are doing: if you have already counted all the individual ions and added up their concentrations to get \(c\), you do not need \(i\) because it is already accounted for. The two approaches give the same answer. 3.4.2 Why does this matter? Isotonicity Osmotic pressure is critically important in biology. Cell membranes are semi-permeable, so if you place a cell in a solution with the wrong osmotic pressure, water flows across the membrane: Too dilute (hypotonic): water flows into the cell, it swells and may burst (lysis). Too concentrated (hypertonic): water flows out of the cell, it shrivels (crenation). A solution with the same osmotic pressure as body fluids is called isotonic. This is why medical solutions like Phosphate-Buffered Saline (PBS) are carefully formulated to match the osmotic pressure of blood (\(\sim 800\) kPa at body temperature). The phosphate component also acts as a pH buffer near physiological pH (\(\sim 7.4\)). 3.5 Electrochemical cells 3.5.1 The physical setup An electrochemical cell consists of two half cells, each containing a chemical species that can gain or lose electrons. The half cells are connected by: A wire (external circuit): electrons flow through this from one electrode to the other. A salt bridge: ions flow through this to maintain electrical neutrality in each half cell. The key physical idea is that the oxidation and reduction are separated in space. Instead of the electron transfer happening directly between the reactants (as it would if you dropped iron into acid), the electrons are forced to travel through the external circuit, where we can measure a voltage or extract useful work. 3.5.2 Cell notation The cell is written as: \[\text{left electrode} \mid \text{left solution} \| \text{right solution} \mid \text{right electrode}\] \(\mid\) = phase boundary (solid/liquid, liquid/gas, etc.) \(\|\) = salt bridge Commas separate species in the same phase. 3.5.3 Reduction potentials: what do they mean? Each half cell has a standard reduction potential \(E^\circ\), listed in data tables. These are written as reduction reactions by convention: \[\text{Oxidised form} + n\,\ce{e-} \longrightarrow \text{Reduced form}\] What does the number mean physically? A more positive \(E^\circ\) means the species has a stronger tendency to gain electrons (be reduced). A more negative \(E^\circ\) means it would rather lose electrons (be oxidised). These are the same reactions that occur in the half cells, and they can run in either direction. The data table writes them as reductions by convention, but in a real cell one half cell will run as a reduction and the other will run in reverse (as an oxidation). Which way round? The cell potential tells us. 3.5.4 Calculating the cell potential This is the central calculation, and it is simple: \[E_\text{cell} = E^\circ(\text{RHS}) - E^\circ(\text{LHS})\] Use the reduction potentials directly from the table. There is no need to flip any reactions or change the sign of any potential. Just subtract: right minus left. The sign of \(E_\text{cell}\) tells you the direction of spontaneous reaction: \(E_\text{cell} > 0\): the reaction proceeds spontaneously as written (left to right). Electrons flow from the left electrode to the right through the external circuit. \(E_\text{cell} < 0\): the spontaneous direction is the reverse. 3.5.5 Anode and cathode The anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs (electrons are released). The cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs (electrons are consumed). One approach to electrochemistry problems is to assign the anode and cathode at the start, using a memorised convention, and then work through the problem from there. This works, but it does rely on remembering the convention correctly, and on the question following the same convention you learnt. An alternative is to let the physics do the work for you. The cell potential \(E_\text{cell}\) tells you, unambiguously, which direction the electrons flow. This tells you where oxidation and reduction occur, which in turn tells you which electrode is the anode and which is the cathode. You do need to remember what “anode” and “cathode” mean, but you do not need to memorise which electrode is which in advance. The physics tells you that. Calculate \(E_\text{cell}\) first. This tells you the direction of electron flow, and therefore where oxidation and reduction occur. The anode and cathode labels then follow from the definitions. 3.5.6 Stoichiometry and \(\Delta G\) To write the balanced overall reaction, you need to multiply the half reactions so that the number of electrons cancels. Getting the stoichiometry right matters, because it determines \(n\), the number of electrons transferred, which you need for \(\Delta G\). However, the cell potential \(E\) itself does not change when you multiply a half reaction. Why not? Because \(E\) is an intensive property: it is the energy per electron transferred. Just as doubling the amount of water in a beaker does not change its temperature, doubling the stoichiometry does not change the voltage. The Gibbs free energy change, on the other hand, is extensive, and scales with the amount of material: \[\Delta G = -nFE\] where \(n\) is the number of moles of electrons transferred in the balanced reaction, and \(F = 96500~\text{C mol}^{-1}\) is Faraday’s constant. If you double the stoichiometry, \(n\) doubles, and \(\Delta G\) doubles. This makes physical sense: reacting twice as much material releases twice as much energy. So: stoichiometry matters for the overall reaction and for \(\Delta G\), but not for \(E\). 3.6 From cell potential to mass: Faraday’s law If a galvanic cell is connected to an external circuit with some resistance, electrons flow and we can work out exactly how much material reacts. The reasoning is a chain of simple steps, each using a single physical law or definition: Cell potential \(\to\) current (Ohm’s law): \[I = \frac{V}{R}\] The cell potential \(V\) drives a current \(I\) through the external resistance \(R\). An amp is a coulomb per second, so this tells you the rate at which charge flows. Current \(\to\) total charge (definition of current): \[Q = I \times t\] If the current flows for time \(t\), the total charge that has passed through the circuit is \(Q\). Charge \(\to\) moles of electrons (Faraday’s constant): \[\text{moles of electrons} = \frac{Q}{F}\] Faraday’s constant \(F = 96500~\text{C mol}^{-1}\) is the charge carried by one mole of electrons. So dividing the total charge by \(F\) gives the number of moles of electrons that have flowed. Moles of electrons \(\to\) moles of substance (stoichiometry): \[\text{moles of substance} = \frac{\text{moles of electrons}}{n}\] Here \(n\) comes directly from the half-reaction. For example, \(\ce{Fe -> Fe^{2+} + 2e-}\) has \(n = 2\): each iron atom releases 2 electrons, so you need 2 moles of electrons to dissolve 1 mole of iron. Moles \(\to\) mass (molar mass): Multiply by the molar mass to get the answer in grams. The logic is completely linear: \[\text{voltage} \longrightarrow \text{current} \longrightarrow \text{charge} \longrightarrow \text{moles of } e^- \longrightarrow \text{moles} \longrightarrow \text{mass}\] Each step uses one definition or law. If you understand what each quantity means physically, you can reconstruct this chain from scratch rather than memorising a formula. 3.6.1 Assumptions to be aware of Real galvanic cells are more complicated than this simple chain suggests. Some assumptions we are making: No internal resistance: We assumed all the resistance is in the external circuit. In reality, the solution has some resistance too. Ions moving through solution have to push past solvent molecules, which impedes the flow of charge. This would reduce the current. Constant voltage: As the reaction proceeds, the concentrations change, which changes the cell potential. We assumed the reaction time is short enough that this effect is negligible. (A more complete treatment uses the Nernst equation.) Ideal solution: We used standard reduction potentials, which assume all activities are 1. In a real solution, activity coefficients would slightly alter the voltage (as discussed in Section 3).

5 Kinetics 5.1 Rate equations and stoichiometry 5.1.1 Rate laws and integrated rate laws Before we get into stoichiometry, it is worth being clear about two things that look similar but answer different questions. A rate law tells you the rate of reaction right now, given the current concentrations. For a first-order elementary process \(\ce{A} \overset{k}{\longrightarrow} \ce{products}\), the rate law is: \[
u = k[\ce{A}]\] An integrated rate law tells you how the concentration changes over time. For the same reaction: \[[\ce{A}]_t = [\ce{A}]_0 \, e^{-kt}\] These are related (the second comes from integrating the first), but they answer different questions. If a problem asks you for the rate in terms of [A], it is asking for the rate law, not the integrated form. 5.1.2 Connecting the rate to individual species For an elementary process, the rate law follows directly from the molecularity: A unimolecular process \(\ce{A -> products}\) has rate \(
u = k[\ce{A}]\). A bimolecular process \(\ce{A + B -> products}\) has rate \(
u = k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]\). A bimolecular process \(\ce{2A -> products}\) has rate \(
u = k[\ce{A}]^2\). Notice that in every case the rate law is written in terms of the reactant concentrations. This is because the rate of an elementary process depends on how often the reactant molecules encounter each other (or, for a unimolecular process, on how many reactant molecules are available to react). Product concentrations do not appear in the rate law for an elementary process. The place where errors often creep in is connecting the overall rate \(
u\) to the rates of change of individual species, \(\mathrm{d}[\ce{X}]/\mathrm{d}t\). Stoichiometric coefficients can appear in two different roles, and it is easy to confuse them. 5.1.3 Powers vs. prefactors When writing rate equations, a stoichiometric coefficient can appear in two different places, for two different reasons: As a power in the rate law (\(
u = k[\ce{A}]^2\)). This answers the question: how many molecules of A need to come together for a single reaction event to happen? As a prefactor relating \(\mathrm{d}[\ce{X}]/\mathrm{d}t\) to the overall rate \(
u\). This answers a different question: how many molecules of X are consumed or produced in each reaction event? These are different questions, and they do not always give the same answer. To see why, it helps to start with a simple case and then look at where the 2:1 stoichiometries cause confusion. The simple case: \(\ce{A} \overset{k}{\longrightarrow} \ce{B}\). This is unimolecular, so one molecule of A is involved in each event. The rate law is \(
u = k[\ce{A}]\). Each event consumes one A and produces one B, so: \[ rac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{A}]}{\mathrm{d}t} = -

It appears as a prefactor on \(\mathrm{d}[\ce{X}]/\mathrm{d}t\) when it tells you how many molecules of that species are consumed or produced per event. If you find one form more intuitive than the other, use that one and rearrange. 5.2 Order and molecularity These terms come up together so often that it is worth being clear about what each one means and where they differ. Order (with respect to a species) is the power to which its concentration is raised in the empirical rate law \(
u = k[\ce{A}]^a[\ce{B}]^b\ldots\) The order with respect to A is \(a\); the overall order is \(a + b + \ldots\) Order is determined experimentally. It does not have to be an integer. Molecularity is the number of reactant molecules (or atoms) involved in an elementary process. A unimolecular process involves one molecule; a bimolecular process involves two. Molecularity is always a positive integer. The important thing to remember is that molecularity is only defined for elementary processes. If a reaction proceeds through a multi-step mechanism, the individual steps each have a molecularity, but the overall reaction does not. The overall reaction has an order (determined by experiment), which can be anything, including non-integer values. For a single elementary process, the molecularity and the overall order are always equal: a bimolecular process is always second-order overall. But for a complex mechanism, the overall order tells you nothing directly about the molecularity of any individual step. 5.3 Testing kinetic models against data Suppose you have measured how the concentration of a reactant changes with time, and you want to work out the order of the reaction. How do you approach this? The idea is to compare your data against the predictions of different kinetic models. Each candidate order (zeroth, first, second…) predicts a specific mathematical relationship between concentration and time. If your data match one of these relationships, you have found the order. The general strategy is described in the lecture notes on methods for determining rate laws, but the logic is: Propose a candidate order (e.g. first-order). Write down the integrated rate law for that order. Rearrange it into the form \(y = mx + c\). Test whether your data are consistent with a straight line when plotted in this form. If the plot is linear, you have found the order, and the slope gives you the rate constant. If the plot is curved, try the next candidate. 5.3.1 The integrated rate laws Each order has a characteristic integrated rate law and a corresponding linear plot: Order Integrated rate law Plot \(y\) vs. \(x\) Slope 0 \([\ce{A}]_t = [\ce{A}]_0 - kt\) \([\ce{A}]_t\) vs. \(t\) \(-k\) 1 \(\ln[\ce{A}]_t = \ln[\ce{A}]_0 - kt\) \(\ln[\ce{A}]_t\) vs. \(t\) \(-k\) 2 \(\displaystyle rac{1}{[\ce{A}]_t} =  rac{1}{[\ce{A}]_0} + kt\) \(1/[\ce{A}]_t\) vs. \(t\) \(k\) These are derived in Lecture 2 by integrating the differential rate equation in each case. 5.3.2 An alternative to plotting: checking consistency You do not always need to draw a graph. You can test a proposed order by substituting two or more data points into the integrated rate law and solving for \(k\). If the same value of \(k\) comes out each time, the data are consistent with that order. If you get different values of \(k\) from different data points, the model does not fit. This is really the same test as plotting: if the data fall on a straight line, the slope (and therefore \(k\)) is the same between any two points. Checking consistency just skips the drawing. 5.3.3 A useful shortcut: the half-life test For a first-order reaction, the half-life is: \[t_{1/2} =  rac{\ln 2}{k}\] Notice that this is independent of concentration. So if a reaction is first-order, the time it takes for the concentration to halve is the same regardless of where you start. You can check this directly from the data without plotting anything: pick any two equal-length time intervals and see whether the concentration drops by the same fraction each time. If the fractional decrease varies with concentration, the reaction is not first-order. For a second-order reaction, the half-life gets longer as the reaction proceeds (because \(t_{1/2} = 1/(k[\ce{A}]_0)\) depends on concentration), so the reaction appears to slow down more than you would expect from first-order kinetics. For a zeroth-order reaction, the half-life gets shorter. 5.3.4 When the data give you products, not reactants Sometimes the experimental data report the concentration of a product rather than a reactant. All of the integrated rate laws above are written in terms of the reactant concentration, so you need to convert. If the stoichiometry is \(\ce{A -> P}\), then every molecule of P that appears came from an A that was consumed, so \([\ce{A}]_t = [\ce{A}]_0 - [\ce{P}]_t\). To use this you need \([\ce{A}]_0\), which you can get from the completion value: when the reaction finishes (\(t = \infty\)), all A has been consumed, so \([\ce{P}]_\infty = [\ce{A}]_0\). 5.4 The isolation method What if the reaction involves more than one reactant? The rate law might be \(
u = k[\ce{A}]^a[\ce{B}]^b\), and you want to find \(a\) and \(b\) separately. The problem is that both concentrations are changing at the same time, which makes it hard to untangle the individual contributions. The isolation method gets around this by using a large excess of one reactant. If \([\ce{B}]_0 \gg [\ce{A}]_0\), then even when all of A has been consumed, [B] has barely changed: \([\ce{B}]_t \approx [\ce{B}]_0\) throughout the reaction. The rate law simplifies to: \[
u = k[\ce{A}]^a[\ce{B}]_0^b = k'[\ce{A}]^a\] where \(k' = k[\ce{B}]_0^b\) is a pseudo-rate-constant that bundles together \(k\) and the (approximately constant) concentration of the excess reactant. The reaction now looks like it only depends on [A], and you can determine \(a\) using the methods above. Once you have determined \(k'\) (from the slope of your linear plot, or by checking consistency), you are not quite finished. The pseudo-rate-constant \(k'\) still has the excess concentration baked into it. To recover the true rate constant \(k\), you need to divide out the contribution from the excess species: \[k =  rac{k'}{[\ce{B}]_0^b}\] If you know \(b\) (e.g. from the stoichiometry or from a separate experiment where you isolate B instead), this is a single division. It is easy to overlook this final step, especially if the analysis of the [A] data took most of the effort. A fuller discussion is in the lecture notes on the isolation method. 5.5 The steady-state approximation The steady-state approximation (SSA) is a technique for simplifying the kinetics of multi-step reactions. It is covered in Lecture 5. Here we focus on the physical reasoning behind it, and on a subtlety in the language that can lead to confusion. 5.5.1 The physical picture Many reaction mechanisms involve a reactive intermediate: a species that is produced in one step and consumed in a subsequent step. If the intermediate is highly reactive, it is consumed almost as soon as it is formed. Its concentration rises quickly to a low value, and then stays approximately constant for most of the reaction. This is the physical basis for the SSA. Because the intermediate is so reactive, its concentration stays low and approximately constant. But think about what “approximately constant” means mathematically: for the concentration to remain steady, the total rate at which the intermediate is formed must be approximately equal to the total rate at which it is consumed. If formation outpaced consumption, the concentration would be rising; if consumption outpaced formation, it would be falling. The steady-state approximation sets \(\mathrm{d}[\ce{I}]/\mathrm{d}t = 0\) for a reactive intermediate I. The physical picture is that the intermediate is so reactive that its concentration stays low and approximately constant. The mathematical condition is that the rate of formation equals the rate of consumption. It is worth being careful with the language here. Each individual molecule of the intermediate has a short lifetime: it is produced and then quickly consumed. This is why the concentration stays low. But the rates (molecules per unit time per unit volume) of formation and consumption must be approximately equal for the concentration to be steady. These two ideas are not contradictory: each molecule is short-lived, but new ones keep being produced at the same rate as old ones are consumed. 5.5.2 Applying the SSA Once you have the physical picture, the procedure for applying the SSA is straightforward: Write down the differential rate equation for every species, including all intermediates. For each reactive intermediate, set \(\mathrm{d}[\ce{I}]/\mathrm{d}t = 0\). Solve algebraically for the concentration of each intermediate in terms of the reactant and product concentrations and the rate constants. Substitute these expressions into the rate equation for the species you care about (usually a reactant or product). The result is a rate law that involves only observable species (reactants, products) and rate constants. The intermediate concentrations have been eliminated. 5.5.3 SSA vs. pre-equilibrium The SSA is not the only way to handle reactive intermediates. Another common approach is the pre-equilibrium approximation, and it is important not to mix them up. In a pre-equilibrium, the first step is a fast, reversible reaction that reaches equilibrium before the second step has time to proceed significantly. You can then write an equilibrium constant \(K = k_1/k_{-1}\) for the first step and use it to express the intermediate concentration in terms of the reactants. This works when the first step is fast and reversible, and the second step is slow. The SSA is different. It does not assume the first step is at equilibrium. Instead, it assumes the intermediate concentration is approximately constant, which requires the rates of formation and consumption to be approximately equal. The SSA is more general: it works whether or not the first step is reversible, and it does not require any particular step to be “fast” or “slow” relative to the others. Both methods can give the same result in certain limits, but they start from different assumptions. If a question asks you to use the SSA, set \(\mathrm{d}[\ce{I}]/\mathrm{d}t = 0\) and solve. Do not write down an equilibrium constant for the first step unless you are told to use a pre-equilibrium approach. 5.6 Simplifying complex rate laws: limiting cases The SSA (and other approaches) sometimes gives rate laws that look more complicated than a simple power law. For example, a mechanism might give: \[ rac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{P}]}{\mathrm{d}t} =  rac{k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]^{1/2}}{1 + k'[\ce{A}]}\] This does not have a simple overall order, because of the \([\ce{A}]\) term in the denominator. But in certain limiting cases, one term in the denominator dominates, and the expression simplifies to something where order is well-defined. 5.6.1 How to find limiting cases The key idea is simple. When you have a sum in the denominator, like \(a + b\), one of the two terms might be much larger than the other. If so, you can drop the smaller term: If \(a \gg b\), then \(a + b \approx a\), and you can ignore \(b\). If \(b \gg a\), then \(a + b \approx b\), and you can ignore \(a\). Let us apply this to the rate law above. The denominator is \(1 + k'[\ce{A}]\), so the two terms are \(1\) and \(k'[\ce{A}]\). If \(k'[\ce{A}] \gg 1\): The denominator becomes \(\approx k'[\ce{A}]\), so: \[ rac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{P}]}{\mathrm{d}t} \approx  rac{k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]^{1/2}}{k'[\ce{A}]} =  rac{k}{k'}[\ce{B}]^{1/2}\] The \([\ce{A}]\) cancels, so the reaction is zeroth-order in A and half-order in B. If \(k'[\ce{A}] \ll 1\): The denominator becomes \(\approx 1\), so: \[ rac{\mathrm{d}[\ce{P}]}{\mathrm{d}t} \approx k[\ce{A}][\ce{B}]^{1/2}\] Now the reaction is first-order in A and half-order in B. A complex rate law may not have a well-defined overall order. But in limiting cases, where one term in the denominator is much larger than the other, it can simplify to a power-law form where order is well-defined. The conditions that determine which limit applies are usually about relative concentrations or rate constants. 5.6.2 A note on molecularity In both limiting cases above, the simplified rate law has a well-defined order. But the overall reaction still does not have a molecularity. Molecularity describes individual elementary steps in the underlying mechanism, not the overall reaction. We can assign an order to the overall reaction (in each limiting case), but only the elementary steps have a molecularity.
